findings.title: New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface, but order() was added as an abstract method rather than a default method. Every existing third-party or downstream implementation that does not define order() will now fail to compile, and already-compiled implementations loaded through ServiceLoader will fail with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts providers. Give order() a default implementation (for example returning 100) so existing providers remain source- and binary-compatible.

findings.title: Equal provider orders make selection between FIPS and non-FIPS providers nondeterministic
findings.body: Providers are now sorted only by order() and the first entry is silently selected instead of failing when multiple providers are present. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when two of them are on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order preserved by the stable sort. In particular a deployment expecting the FIPS provider can silently start with the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider, losing FIPS compliance without any error. The previously strict multiple-provider failure should be retained for equal highest orders, or the built-in providers need distinct, documented priorities with deterministic tie-breaking.

findings.title: AuthzClient creation can permanently install the minimal Authz provider as the JVM-wide crypto provider
findings.body: Every AuthzClient.create(Configuration) call now initializes the static, initialize-once CryptoIntegration singleton. In a JVM where AuthzClientCryptoProvider is the only provider visible to AuthzClient's classloader at that moment, it becomes the global provider for the lifetime of the JVM; later CryptoIntegration.init calls with a fuller provider are no-ops. Subsequent code using CryptoIntegration for PEM handling, signatures, key factories, certificate utilities, AES ciphers, or ECDSA getPublicFromPrivate will then fail with UnsupportedOperationException from AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead of using a full provider that becomes available or is initialized later.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an arbitrary JCA provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is contracted to return the BouncyCastle (or BC-FIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is typically a JDK provider such as SUN/SunJCE and is unrelated to BouncyCastle. Callers that pass this provider to BouncyCastle-specific APIs, check its name against CryptoConstants.BC_PROVIDER_ID, or rely on BC algorithm availability can fail or silently use different cryptography. The method should either return a real BC provider if one is available or signal that it is unsupported, not mislabel the default KeyStore provider.

findings.title: ECDSA tests reuse one default-curve key pair for ES256, ES384 and ES512 and never verify the converted signature
findings.body: The test generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() (the JDK default curve) and uses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512, whose JOSE signature lengths correspond to P-256, P-384 and P-521. It then only asserts that converting DER -> concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS preserves the concatenated bytes, without checking the expected R/S component lengths for each curve or verifying the re-encoded DER signature against the public key. Bugs in handling leading zero bytes or component truncation/padding for real P-384/P-521 signatures can therefore pass unnoticed. Generate a key pair on the correct curve per algorithm and verify the DER round-trip with java.security.Signature.
